title: A maintenance plan after launch
metaTitle: A maintenance plan with an owner
excerpt: Name who will update the framework, watch the forms, and renew the domain after launch. A site with no owner for the next year starts decaying as soon as the project ends.
alt: A hand holding a stylus over a tablet covered in wireframe sketches, with a keyboard and mouse beside it. The sketch is the start. Someone still has to keep the built site current.
caption: Sketches on the tablet, and the tools to keep going. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Who should own a site after launch?
faqs.answer: One named person, with a backup, who can get into the repository, the host, the registrar, and the form inbox. The team is not an owner. The owner does the small monthly work and calls for help on a major upgrade or an outage. If a studio built the site, the company still needs the logins, or the site is rented from someone's memory.

faqs.question: What belongs on a monthly maintenance pass?
faqs.answer: Routine dependency updates on staging, a test of the form including the spam folder, a check that the domain and the bills will renew, and a look at the top pages for outdated offers. Major framework upgrades deserve their own window twice a year. Security patches skip the queue.

faqs.question: How do Core Web Vitals fit a maintenance plan?
faqs.answer: Watch the field numbers, not a one-time lab score. The Web Vitals documentation calls a good experience an LCP within two and a half seconds, an INP within two hundred milliseconds, and a CLS at or below one tenth, read at the 75th percentile of page loads. When a new script or a huge image pushes the real pages off those marks, maintenance includes taking it back off.

sources.title: Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google search results

markdown:
A website maintenance plan names the person who will keep the site alive after launch: update the framework, watch the forms, and renew the domain. A launch without an owner for the next year starts decaying on day two. The decay is quiet. A form that stops arriving. A certificate that lapses. A dependency that falls behind until the upgrade is no longer small.

Write the plan before the launch week, when people still remember who has the logins. A plan written after the first outage is a postmortem. Useful, and late.

## An owner, not a vibe

Name a person. They can be inside the company or at the studio, and they can have backup, but one name is accountable. “The team” will assume someone else saw the renewal email. The owner’s job is to notice, to do the small work, and to call for help on the large work before it is an emergency.

Write what they own this year.

- Domain registration and DNS
- Hosting, certificates, and the bill for each
- Framework and dependency updates
- The form path, from the button to a person
- Accounts: CMS, analytics, registrar, repository
- A short list of what “broken” means for this site

If a studio built it, the owner still needs the repository, the deployment, and the content logins. A site you cannot enter is not maintained. It is rented from whoever remembers the password. Hanabi’s builds are in code the client can own: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind, on Vercel, with Prisma and PostgreSQL when the project has a database. The plan should say where that code lives and who may merge.

Decide the hours. Maintenance is not a promise to redesign on a Sunday night. It is a promise that a failed form on a Tuesday is seen on Tuesday, and that updates happen on a cadence you chose, not only when something is on fire.

## The framework and the small updates

Set a cadence. Monthly is enough for most marketing sites if someone actually does the month. Open the dependency list, apply the updates that are routine, and run the site. Look at the homepage, the key template, and the form. Ship if it is healthy. Write down what you deferred and why.

Major upgrades are not the monthly chore. A large framework jump deserves its own window, a staging deploy, and a person who can roll back. Put that window on the calendar twice a year so it is a plan, not a surprise forced by a security release on a holiday.

Read the release notes for anything that touches forms, images, or authentication. Those are the usual places a “small” update changes behavior. If you do not have time to read, you do not have time to update blindly. Schedule the hour.

Keep a staging environment that resembles production. Test the update there first. A maintenance plan that updates production because there is no staging will eventually update the homepage into a blank page. Staging is part of the cost of owning the site. Include it.

Security releases skip the cadence. If the owner sees a notice that says to patch now, they patch, or they call the person who can, the same day. The plan should say who that person is when the owner is away. A named backup is the difference between a patch and a forwarded email.

## Watch the form, the domain, and the certificate

The form is the site’s working part. Once a week, or with a scheduled test submission, confirm that a message reaches the person who replies. Check the spam folder of that inbox as well as the happy path. A change at the email provider can break delivery without breaking the button. The sender still saw a thank-you. You saw nothing.

Uptime is the blunt version of the same watch. You do not need a large program. You need to know if the homepage returns an error, and you need the note to reach a person who can act. Tie the alert to the owner, not to a channel everyone muted.

Domain renewal is a calendar event with a reminder weeks ahead, on more than one person’s calendar. Auto-renew is fine if the card is valid and someone checks that it worked. An expired card on the registrar is enough to take a site dark. You do not need a published statistic to put the renewal on a calendar. It is a failure mode you can see coming. The same for the hosting bill and the email bill. Add them to the same list.

Certificates are often automatic and still worth a glance after DNS changes. If you move a record, test the URL on a phone that is not already logged into your own machine’s exceptions. HTTPS that fails only for strangers is a launch-day classic that also happens in March because someone “just” added a subdomain.

DNS access should be documented. Where the records live, who can edit them, and which records must not be touched because they serve mail. A maintenance plan that says “update the site” and locks the team out of DNS will stall the first time you need a new record. Share the access as a role, and remove people who leave.

## Content, performance, and the quiet rot

Someone should know how to change a headline, a price, and a team member without a developer, if that was the promise at launch. If every sentence requires a deploy, the plan should say that, and the owner should be someone who can make that deploy safely. Do not imply the marketing team can edit what the CMS does not expose.

Broken links and outdated offers are maintenance. A campaign that ended in December and still says it is open in June is a defect. A quarterly pass through the top templates is enough for a small site. Look at dates, prices, names, and the primary call to action. Remove what is no longer true.

Performance is part of the watch, not a one-time launch score. Google’s [Core Web Vitals](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-web-vitals) are the field measures tied to search: how fast the main content shows, how quickly the page responds to input, and how much the layout shifts. web.dev’s [Web Vitals](https://web.dev/articles/vitals) documentation sets the current “good” thresholds at an LCP of 2.5 seconds or less, an INP of 200 milliseconds or less, and a CLS of 0.1 or less, read at the 75th percentile of visits. You do not need to chase a perfect lab score every month. You do need to notice when a new script, a huge image, or a font change pushes the real pages out of that range.

When the numbers move, look for the change you made. A chat widget, an unoptimized hero, a third-party embed. Maintenance includes the right to remove what the plan did not approve. A homepage that accumulates scripts is how a fast launch becomes a slow site without a redesign.

Accessibility fixes belong on the same list as functional bugs. A label that disappeared, a contrast that failed after a color tweak, a focus state that a refresh removed. The owner does not have to be an auditor. They have to treat those breaks as broken, and schedule them with the other defects.

## What the year should cost attention, not heroics

A small marketing site, kept well, is a few hours a month plus the twice-yearly upgrade window. A shop or a product with accounts is more, because payments, data, and dependencies have more ways to fail. Down the Cove’s public scope, an ecommerce migration and redesign, implies a heavier watch than a brand site with a handful of templates. Say which one you are maintaining. Do not price a shop like a brochure, and do not staff a brochure like a crisis.

Write a monthly checklist that fits on half a page. Updates considered. Form tested. Domain and bills alive. Top pages still true. Vitals not wildly worse than last month. Backups, if you have a database, actually restorable. If the checklist becomes a project plan, you have mixed new features into maintenance. Features are a separate yes.

New work can be a retainer or a quote. The maintenance plan should say how a request becomes one or the other. “Change the phone number” is maintenance. “Add a journal with six templates” is a project. The owner may do the phone number. They should not silently absorb the journal.

Incidents get a short note: what failed, what you did, what you will change in the checklist. You are building a memory. The next owner, or the same owner in eight months, should not have to rediscover that a particular integration drops mail.

If the studio remains involved, say the response window. Same week for defects in the agreed pages. A separate schedule for new templates. A window is kinder than “just ping us,” which means whoever happens to see chat. Hanabi’s ongoing help, when you want it, should be as explicit as the build was.

## Leave the next person a map

The plan is also a document. Where the repo is, how to deploy, how to roll back, where the environment variables live, who the registrar is, how the form is wired, where the analytics property sits. Store it next to the code and give the owner a copy outside the single laptop that built the site.

Include the content model. Which fields exist, which pages are templates, what not to paste into the CMS from a design tool. A year of random paste is its own kind of outage. It makes the next real update expensive.

Review the plan when something structural changes. A new product name, a new domain, a move off a vendor. The day you change it, change the document. A map of last year’s architecture is how a well-meaning editor breaks production.

Then run one drill. Ask the backup owner to find the form test and the rollback steps without calling the person who wrote them. The gaps in that drill are the real plan, still unwritten. Fill them while the launch is fresh.

The site you are maintaining still has to prove something on the first screen. [What the homepage has to prove for a B2B SaaS company](/blog/what-the-homepage-has-to-prove-for-a-b2b-saas-company) is the next piece if the thing you are keeping alive is a product homepage, because maintenance cannot rescue a first screen that never said what the product does.

If you want the build and the year after it scoped as one conversation, see [Hanabi’s services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The useful plan is the one that names an owner before the launch party.
